Create source-grounded retrieval evaluation questions. Return JSON {"items":[...]}.
For EACH supplied source return {"id":same id,"en":English patient question,"zh":Chinese patient question,
"evidence_id":the exact id string of ONE supplied evidence_options entry supporting BOTH questions}.
Ask one concrete question about a supported detail (cause, symptom, prevention, evaluation, management).
The two questions express the SAME information need, not two facts. Use ordinary patient language.
Include enough topic context to identify the condition but do not copy a source sentence into the question.
Select an evidence option and ask about a concrete detail stated in that option. Do not ask for a personalized dose or individual diagnosis. Do not invent content. No answers in questions.
These are synthetic topic-source retrieval labels, not a clinician-authored benchmark.

[{"id": "MLP-5383", "title": "Vitamin D", "evidence_options": [{"id": "S000", "text": "Vitamins are substances that your body needs to grow and develop normally."}, {"id": "S001", "text": "Vitamin D is important to your body because: It helps your body absorb calcium ."}, {"id": "S002", "text": "Calcium is one of the main building blocks of bone."}, {"id": "S003", "text": "A lack of vitamin D can lead to bone diseases such as osteoporosis or rickets ."}, {"id": "S004", "text": "It also has a role in your nerve, muscle, and immune systems: Your muscles need it to move Your nerves need it to carry messages between your brain and your body Your immune system needs vitamin D to fight off bacteria and viruses How do I get vitamin D?"}, {"id": "S005", "text": "You can get vitamin D in three ways: through your skin, from your diet, and from supplements."}, {"id": "S006", "text": "Your body forms vitamin D naturally after exposure to sunlight ."}, {"id": "S007", "text": "However, too much sun exposure can lead to skin aging and skin cancer ."}, {"id": "S008", "text": "So many people try to get their vitamin D from other sources."}, {"id": "S009", "text": "Very few foods naturally contain vitamin D."}, {"id": "S010", "text": "Most people get vitamin D in their diet from foods that are fortified."}, {"id": "S011", "text": "This means that vitamin D is added to the food."}, {"id": "S012", "text": "These foods may include milk, cereal, and yogurt."}, {"id": "S013", "text": "Foods that naturally have vitamin D include egg yolks, saltwater fish, and liver."}, {"id": "S014", "text": "It is also included in many multivitamins."}, {"id": "S015", "text": "The two forms of vitamin D in supplements are D2 and D3."}, {"id": "S016", "text": "Both types increase vitamin D in your blood, but D3 might raise it higher and for longer than D2."}, {"id": "S017", "text": "You can absorb it better when you take your supplements with a meal or snack that includes some fat."}, {"id": "S018", "text": "The amount of vitamin D you need each day depends on your age."}, {"id": "S019", "text": "The recommended amounts, in international units (IU), are: Birth to 12 months: 400 IU Children 1-13 years: 600 IU Teens 14-18 years: 600 IU Adults 19-70 years: 600 IU Adults 71 years and older: 800 IU If you are pregnant or breastfeeding: 600 IU But certain people may need extra vitamin D, such as: Older adults Breastfed infants People with dark skin People with certain conditions that limit the absorption of fat, such as Crohn's disease , celiac disease , and ulcerative colitis People who have obesity or have had gastric bypass surgery Check with your health care provider to see if you need to take vitamin D supplements, and if so, how much you should take."}, {"id": "S020", "text": "Your provider may want to first do a vitamin D test to see if you are getting enough of it."}, {"id": "S021", "text": "NIH: National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements"}]}, {"id": "MLP-154", "title": "Autoimmune Diseases", "evidence_options": [{"id": "S000", "text": "Your immune system protects you from disease and infection by attacking germs that get into your body, such as viruses and bacteria."}, {"id": "S001", "text": "Your immune system can tell that the germs aren't part of you, so it destroys them."}, {"id": "S002", "text": "If you have an autoimmune disease, your immune system attacks the healthy cells of your organs and tissues by mistake."}, {"id": "S003", "text": "There are more than 80 types of autoimmune diseases."}, {"id": "S004", "text": "They can affect almost any part of your body."}, {"id": "S005", "text": "For example, alopecia areata is an autoimmune disease of the skin that causes hair loss."}, {"id": "S006", "text": "In type 1 diabetes , the immune system attacks the pancreas."}, {"id": "S007", "text": "And in rheumatoid arthritis , the immune system can attack many parts of the body, including the joints, lungs, and eyes."}, {"id": "S008", "text": "No one is sure why autoimmune diseases happen."}, {"id": "S009", "text": "But you can't catch them from other people."}, {"id": "S010", "text": "Autoimmune diseases do tend to run in families, which means that certain genes may make some people more likely to develop a problem."}, {"id": "S011", "text": "Viruses, certain chemicals, and other things in the environment may trigger an autoimmune disease if you already have the genes for it."}, {"id": "S012", "text": "Millions of Americans of all ages have autoimmune diseases."}, {"id": "S013", "text": "Women develop many types of autoimmune diseases much more often than men."}, {"id": "S014", "text": "And if you have one autoimmune disease, you are more likely to get another."}, {"id": "S015", "text": "What are the symptoms of autoimmune diseases?"}, {"id": "S016", "text": "The symptoms of an autoimmune disease depend on the part of your body that's affected."}, {"id": "S017", "text": "Many types of autoimmune diseases cause redness, swelling, heat, and pain, which are the signs and symptoms of inflammation."}, {"id": "S018", "text": "But other illnesses can cause the same symptoms."}, {"id": "S019", "text": "The symptoms of autoimmune diseases can come and go."}, {"id": "S020", "text": "During a flare-up, your symptoms may get severe for a while."}, {"id": "S021", "text": "Later on, you may have a remission, which means that your symptoms get better or disappear for a period of time."}, {"id": "S022", "text": "Doctors often have a hard time diagnosing autoimmune diseases."}, {"id": "S023", "text": "There's usually not a specific test to show whether you have a certain autoimmune disease."}, {"id": "S024", "text": "That's because many autoimmune diseases have similar symptoms."}, {"id": "S025", "text": "And some symptoms, such as muscle aches, are common in many other illnesses."}, {"id": "S026", "text": "So it can take a long time and some visits to different types of doctors to get a diagnosis."}, {"id": "S027", "text": "To help your doctor find out if an autoimmune disease is causing your symptoms,: Learn about the health conditions in your family history ."}, {"id": "S028", "text": "What health problems did your grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins have?"}, {"id": "S029", "text": "Write down what you learn and share it with your doctor."}, {"id": "S030", "text": "Keep track of your symptoms, including how long they last and what makes them better or worse."}, {"id": "S031", "text": "See a specialist who deals with the symptoms that bother you most."}, {"id": "S032", "text": "For example, if you have rash, see a dermatologist (skin doctor)."}, {"id": "S033", "text": "What are the treatments for autoimmune diseases?"}, {"id": "S034", "text": "In most cases, the goal of treatment is to suppress (slow down) your immune system, and ease swelling, redness, and pain from inflammation."}, {"id": "S035", "text": "Your doctor may give you corticosteroids or other medicines to help you feel better."}, {"id": "S036", "text": "For some diseases, you may need treatment for the rest of your life."}]}, {"id": "MLP-1229", "title": "Edema", "evidence_options": [{"id": "S000", "text": "Edema means swelling caused by fluid in your body's tissues."}, {"id": "S001", "text": "It usually occurs in the feet, ankles and legs, but it can involve your entire body."}, {"id": "S002", "text": "Causes of edema include: Eating too much salt Sunburn Heart failure Kidney disease Liver problems from cirrhosis Pregnancy Problems with lymph nodes , especially after mastectomy Some medicines Standing or walking a lot when the weather is warm To keep swelling down, your health care provider may recommend keeping your legs raised when sitting, wearing support stockings, limiting how much salt you eat, or taking a medicine called a diuretic - also called a water pill."}]}, {"id": "MLP-4287", "title": "HIV Medicines", "evidence_options": [{"id": "S000", "text": "HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus."}, {"id": "S001", "text": "It harms your immune system by destroying CD4 cells."}, {"id": "S002", "text": "These are a type of white blood cells that fight infection."}, {"id": "S003", "text": "The loss of these cells makes it hard for your body to fight off infections and certain HIV-related cancers."}, {"id": "S004", "text": "Without treatment, HIV can gradually destroy the immune system and advance to AIDS."}, {"id": "S005", "text": "AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome."}, {"id": "S006", "text": "It is the final stage of infection with HIV."}, {"id": "S007", "text": "The treatment of HIV with medicines is called antiretroviral therapy (ART)."}, {"id": "S008", "text": "It involves taking a combination of medicines every day."}, {"id": "S009", "text": "ART is recommended for everyone who has HIV."}, {"id": "S010", "text": "The medicines do not cure HIV infection, but help people with HIV live longer, healthier lives."}, {"id": "S011", "text": "They also reduce the risk of spreading the virus to others."}, {"id": "S012", "text": "HIV medicines reduce the amount of HIV (viral load) in your body, which helps by: Giving your immune system a chance to recover."}, {"id": "S013", "text": "Even though there is still some HIV in your body, your immune system should be strong enough to fight off infections and certain HIV-related cancers."}, {"id": "S014", "text": "Reducing the risk that you will spread HIV to others."}, {"id": "S015", "text": "There are many different types (called classes) of HIV medicines."}, {"id": "S016", "text": "Some work by blocking or changing enzymes that HIV needs to make copies of itself."}, {"id": "S017", "text": "This prevents HIV from copying itself, which reduces the amount of HIV in the body."}, {"id": "S018", "text": "Several types of medicines do this: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) block an enzyme called reverse transcriptase Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) bind to and later change reverse transcriptase Integrase inhibitors , also called integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), block an enzyme called integrase Protease inhibitors (PIs) block an enzyme called protease Some types of HIV medicines interfere with HIV's ability to infect CD4 immune system cells: Fusion inhibitors block HIV from entering the cells CCR5 antagonists and post-attachment inhibitors block different molecules on the CD4 cells."}, {"id": "S019", "text": "To infect a cell, HIV has to bind to two types of molecules on the cell's surface."}, {"id": "S020", "text": "Blocking either of these molecules prevents HIV from entering the cells."}, {"id": "S021", "text": "Attachment inhibitors bind to a specific protein on the outer surface of HIV."}, {"id": "S022", "text": "This prevents HIV from entering the cell."}, {"id": "S023", "text": "Pharmacokinetic enhancers are another type of medicine."}, {"id": "S024", "text": "They are sometimes taken along with certain other HIV medicines."}, {"id": "S025", "text": "Pharmacokinetic enhancers increase the effectiveness of the other medicine."}, {"id": "S026", "text": "They work by slowing the breakdown of the other medicine."}, {"id": "S027", "text": "This allows that medicine to stay in the body longer at a higher concentration."}, {"id": "S028", "text": "There are also multidrug combinations , which include a combination of two or more different types of HIV medicines."}, {"id": "S029", "text": "When do I need to start taking HIV medicines?"}, {"id": "S030", "text": "It's important to start taking HIV medicines as soon as possible after your diagnosis, especially if you: Are pregnant Have AIDS Have certain HIV-related illnesses and infections Have an early HIV infection (the first 6 months after infection with HIV) What else do I need to know about taking HIV medicines?"}, {"id": "S031", "text": "You and your health care provider will work together to come up with a personal treatment plan."}, {"id": "S032", "text": "This plan will be based on many factors, including: The possible side effects of HIV medicines Potential drug interactions with any other medicines you take How many medicines you will need to take every day Any other health problems you may have It's important to take your medicines every day, according to the instructions from your provider."}, {"id": "S033", "text": "If you miss doses or don't follow a regular schedule, your treatment may not work, and the HIV virus may become resistant to the medicines."}, {"id": "S034", "text": "Most of these side effects are manageable, but a few can be serious."}, {"id": "S035", "text": "Tell your provider about any side effects that you are having."}, {"id": "S036", "text": "Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking to your provider."}, {"id": "S037", "text": "There may be steps you can take to help manage the side effects."}, {"id": "S038", "text": "In some cases, your provider may decide to change your medicines."}, {"id": "S039", "text": "HIV medicines are not just used for treatment."}, {"id": "S040", "text": "PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who don't already have HIV but are at very high risk of getting it."}, {"id": "S041", "text": "PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who have possibly been exposed to HIV."}]}, {"id": "MLP-1237", "title": "Pheochromocytoma", "evidence_options": [{"id": "S000", "text": "Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor that usually starts in the cells of one of your adrenal glands."}, {"id": "S001", "text": "Although they are usually benign , pheochromocytomas often cause the adrenal gland to make too many hormones."}, {"id": "S002", "text": "This can lead to high blood pressure and cause symptoms such as : Headaches Sweating Pounding of the heart Being shaky Being extremely pale Sometimes pheochromocytoma is part of another condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome (MEN)."}, {"id": "S003", "text": "People with MEN often have other cancers and other problems involving hormones."}, {"id": "S004", "text": "Doctors use lab tests and imaging tests to diagnose it."}, {"id": "S005", "text": "Other options include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy."}, {"id": "S006", "text": "Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells."}]}]
